name: Underarm liners

lead: Underarm liners are thin absorbent pads that sit between the armpit and the fabric of a garment. They soak up sweat before it reaches the cloth, so visible wet patches, yellowing and odor build-up in clothing are reduced.
The appearance payoff is a cleaner-looking outfit, especially in light colors, silk or fitted shirts. They are an alternative or addition to antiperspirant and do not change how much a person sweats.

paras: Disposable liners are peel-and-stick: an adhesive plastic-backed side attaches to the inside of the garment and the absorbent paper side faces the armpit. Reusable versions clip to a bra strap, with a cotton layer against the skin and a nylon or vinyl barrier facing the garment. They are used under shirts, dresses and suits, often for events or hot days.

Liners are low risk. Plastic or adhesive backing can irritate sensitive skin or feel warm, and a liner that shifts can show through thin fabric. People with heavy sweating sometimes use them alongside medical treatments for hyperhidrosis.

angle.text: The liner sits between skin and fabric and takes up sweat, so shirts and dresses look dry and clean. It protects the garment and does not alter the body's sweating.

lead: Underarm liners, also called dress shields, underarm pads or sweat guards, are absorbent inserts that attach to the inside of clothing to take up armpit sweat. They are an alternative to chemical antiperspirants and are also used together with them [1].

For looks, the purpose is protecting how the clothing appears: preventing wet patches and sweat stains on shirts and delicate dresses. Before chemical antiperspirants existed, women commonly used liners to protect dresses from stains and fading, and the product persisted alongside modern deodorants [1].

Two forms are common. Reusable liners clip to a bra strap, with a cotton layer facing the skin and a nylon or vinyl barrier facing the garment; they are now less common. Disposable liners are sold for both men and women as a peel-and-stick product, with a plastic adhesive barrier on one side and absorbent paper on the other [1]. No published clinical trials of underarm liners were located.
infobox: Dress shields, underarm pads, sweat guards

paras: Disposable liners have an adhesive plastic barrier that sticks inside the garment and an absorbent paper layer that sits against the armpit [1]. Reusable shields are traditional dress shields that clip to a bra strap, with cotton against the skin and a nylon or vinyl barrier facing the garment [1].

Before chemical antiperspirants, women commonly used liners to keep sweat from staining or fading delicate dresses. Antiperspirants moved from early creams and powders to sticks, sprays and roll-ons, while liners remained available [1].
